title: Political office has remained socially selective across US history
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35569, Fortunate Sons: Elite Political Selection in American History, linking historical Members of Congress and family records
geography: United States; Members of Congress born 1830–1950 and matched historical census records

denominator.unit: Historical Members of Congress and matched census controls; exact public-abstract counts are not retained

economic_origin.value: Future Members of Congress were economic outliers and came from more advantaged families than matched controls

education_gap.value: By 1940, close to 60% of Members aged 18–40 held a college degree versus under 5% of comparable young men outside Congress

family_background_gap.value: The family-background gap held or widened across cohorts; roughly half of the adult economic premium was shared with a brother and half was individual

reform_test.value: Women's suffrage, secret ballot, direct primaries, and direct election of senators produced no detectable shift in who reached Congress in the study's tests

observations.method: The study links Members of Congress, parents, and brothers to complete-count censuses and tests reforms using historical comparisons and close-election designs; this record retains the abstract-level results without reconstructing the full sample or estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The public abstract does not expose all sample construction, measurement choices, effect sizes, or the full set of controls. Historical selection patterns do not identify present-day mechanisms, and a reform null does not prove that institutions never changed access through other channels.
observations.subgroup: Members of Congress by birth cohort, family background, education, wealth, and reform-era comparison; matched controls and exact subgroup counts remain paper-specific.
observations.counterinterpretation: Family resources may reflect education, information, networks, geographic opportunity, or selection into politics rather than a single inherited mechanism. Elite origins do not by themselves show poor representation, corruption, or identical policy views across parties.

related_sources.claim: Repository finding preserves the historical selection result and its transfer boundary.

boundary: This record supports a historical US political-selection pattern: family origin and socioeconomic advantage are overrepresented among Members of Congress, and selected Progressive-Era reforms did not visibly alter that composition in the study's tests. It does not establish current representativeness, present-day causal mechanisms, constituent treatment, policy quality, public trust, or political action by ordinary citizens.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER working-paper landing page and public abstract; full paper, code, historical microdata, and linked census extracts are not retained.
